opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that they're really answering slightly different questions. LLM Modulo was our attempt to say: look, these autoregressive models are wonderful idea generators, but they don't, by themselves, guarantee anything. So rather than pretending they reason, let's put them in a loop with external verifiers, critics that actually check whether a plan or a solution is correct, and let the LLM keep generating candidates while the verifiers give back feedback. The guarantees come from the verifiers, not from the LLM.

O1, and the large reasoning models that followed, take a different tack. They essentially try to internalize some of that generate-and-test process. They're trained, with reinforcement learning on top of the base model, to produce these long sequences of intermediate tokens before giving an answer, and that clearly helps. On planning benchmarks like Blocksworld, and especially the obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" versions where the standard LLMs basically fell apart, we did see real improvements with O1. I want to be fair about that. It's not just autocomplete in the old sense anymore; there's some kind of search-like computation going on at inference time.

But when you compare the two, a few things stand out. One is guarantees. With LLM Modulo, if the verifier says the plan is correct, it's correct, because the verifier is sound. With O1, you get an answer that's often better, but you still don't have any guarantee, and performance degrades as problems get longer or as you add unsolvable instances. It will sometimes confidently tell you a plan exists when it doesn't, and give you something plausible-looking. Those intermediate tokens aren't a proof, and I've been pretty vocal that we shouldn't anthropomorphize them as "thoughts" just because they look like a human's scratch work.

The second is cost. O1 spends a lot of compute on those reasoning tokens, and you're paying for them, often without seeing them. In our experiments, LLM Modulo-style setups, even with cheaper base models, could reach comparable or better accuracy on some of these problems, with a correctness guarantee, at lower cost. And of course, if you really care about Blocksworld, a classical planner solves it essentially perfectly for almost nothing. That's a useful reality check.

So my view is not that one replaces the other. O1-style models are better generators, and better generators make LLM Modulo work better, because you need fewer iterations with the verifier. But for anything where correctness matters, I'd still want that external verification loop. The reasoning model gets you closer, the verifier is what lets you actually trust the answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, so the first thing I'd say is that O1 and LLM-Modulo are actually trying to do related things, but they come at it from very different places, and the differences matter.

LLM-Modulo is this framework we proposed where the LLM is a generator of candidate plans or solutions, and then you have external, sound verifiers, model-based critics, that check those candidates and give feedback, and you iterate. The LLM is doing what it's good at, which is generating plausible stuff, approximate retrieval, if you like, and the verifiers are doing what LLMs are bad at, which is actually guaranteeing correctness. The key is that the guarantees come from the critics, not from the LLM. So if a plan comes out of that loop, you know it's correct, because something with actual semantics has signed off on it.

Now, O1, as far as anyone outside OpenAI can tell, is essentially trying to internalize something like this. It's doing reinforcement learning on reasoning traces, some kind of generate-and-check at training time, maybe at inference time with the extra compute, so that the model gets better at producing chains that lead to correct answers. And you could say, look, that's an LLM-Modulo-like approach where the verifier was used during training and then the whole thing got compiled into the model. I've called these things LRMs, large reasoning models, rather than LLMs, precisely because they are not just doing next token prediction on human text anymore.

So how do I evaluate them against each other? A few points.

First, O1 does do much better on things like Blocksworld than the plain LLMs did. We ran it, and the numbers went up substantially. But they also fall off as the problems get longer, and on the obfuscated versions, Mystery Blocksworld, where you rename the actions so you can't lean on world knowledge, the performance drops again, quite dramatically. So it's not that O1 has somehow acquired a general planning capability. It's gotten better at the distribution it was trained on.

Second, and this is the crucial thing, O1 gives you no guarantees. It gives you an answer with higher accuracy, but it doesn't tell you when it's wrong. Interestingly, it's also not well calibrated about this, it will confidently give you an invalid plan. With LLM-Modulo, when the verifier is sound, you either get a correct solution or you know you don't have one. For a lot of applications, that difference is everything.

Third, cost. O1 is enormously expensive per call, and you don't actually know how much compute it's burning. With LLM-Modulo, you know exactly what's happening, the LLM calls and the verifier calls are explicit, and the verifier is usually cheap. In our experiments the cost comparison was quite striking, and you can get to the same or better accuracy for much less.

So my view is that O1 is sort of a step toward what we've been arguing for, which is that you need generation plus verification. They just chose to bake the verification in at training time, and the result is a model that's better on average but opaque and unreliable. LLM-Modulo keeps the verification external and explicit, which is less sexy but gives you something you can actually trust. And honestly, the two aren't exclusive. You can put O1 inside an LLM-Modulo loop as the generator. It'll just be a better generator, and you'll still want the verifier.

r002.rationale: It describes O1 as expensive and the verifier as usually cheap, but does not state that using a general-purpose reasoning model for work suited to a specialized tool is time-inefficient.

astra-6.text:
I would start by separating generating a plausible solution from establishing that the solution is correct. A language model can be very useful at proposing a plan or a proof. But the fact that it produces a longer chain of reasoning doesn't, by itself, establish correctness.

The idea behind LLM Modulo is to put that generative capability inside a loop with external verifiers. The model proposes a candidate, the verifiers check it, and their feedback helps guide the next proposal. If you have a sound verifier, then an accepted answer comes with whatever guarantees that verifier supports. That doesn't mean the system will always find an answer, and it doesn't mean you've perfectly captured the user's problem in the formal specification. Those are separate issues.

So I wouldn't necessarily view O1 and LLM Modulo as mutually exclusive alternatives. O1 could be the candidate generator in an LLM Modulo system. If it generates better candidates, we might need fewer rounds of verification and revision. The external check still serves a purpose.

For evaluation, I would ask: How many problems do you actually solve correctly, as judged by an independent checker? What is the total computational cost, including candidate generation and verification? And how does performance change when you move beyond familiar problem patterns? You need to compare those things under comparable budgets.

The interesting question is whether additional computation makes the model a better proposer, and how best to combine that proposer with machinery that can reliably check its work.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by separating two questions: can a system produce a useful candidate solution, and can it establish that the solution is correct? Those are quite different capabilities.

The idea behind LLM Modulo is to use the language model to propose candidates, and then have external verifiers check them. If a candidate fails, the verifier provides feedback, and the model can try again. The guarantees, to the extent that you have them, come from the verifier—not from the model sounding confident or producing a long chain of thought.

So, in comparing this with O1, I would ask: what problems are we testing, what constitutes success, and how much computation are we allowing? On a planning problem, for example, I want to check that the proposed plan actually satisfies the constraints and reaches the goal. Getting a plausible-looking sequence of actions is not enough. And I would measure the cost of the entire process, including verification and retries.

But I don’t see these as necessarily competing approaches. A model that is better at generating candidates could be a better component inside an LLM Modulo system. You could put O1 in that loop. The important architectural question is whether we are asking the language model to be both the proposer and the final authority on correctness. I would rather let it propose, and let an appropriate verifier decide.

r002.rationale: The response favors having a verifier decide correctness, but does not observe that using a general-purpose reasoning model for work suited to a specialized tool can waste time.
